spine: Type D is a real research construct, but it was built to predict heart-health outcomes in cardiac patients, its headline mortality finding failed to replicate, and nothing in its evidence base touches job performance. So a hiring manager who thinks they have spotted it in a candidate is working from a label that cannot be assigned in an interview, cannot be defended if challenged, and carries ADA exposure the moment it influences a decision. By the end the reader can drop the label, run a structured, rubric-scored interview that measures job behaviour instead of manner, and manage a guarded or negative-leaning person well once they are on the team.
coverage_note: Left out the day-to-day 'Type D trait portrait' (sad, irritable, pessimistic, organised, persistent) that ranking pages lead with: after this article argues the label cannot be assigned by observation, a spotting guide would contradict it, and those claims come from the same popular framing the piece is correcting. Core traits are still covered, as negative affectivity plus social inhibition in section 1. Left out clinical treatment of Type D (counselling, therapy, mindfulness), which is written for the patient or clinician, not for a hiring manager, and which collides with the ADA point about referring employees to counselling. Google's DiSC 'Dominant' disambiguation is explicitly outside this article's subject and is ignored. Health concerns are covered, but as the research story in section 2 rather than as health advice.

sections.job: Finish what competing pages abandon mid-list. Settle what a manager does once a quiet, negative-leaning person is on the team, worked through one named hire from first week to first feedback, managing the observed behaviour and never the label. list.of: the concrete manager moves, each one a practice applied to the same named team member

needs_research.topic: Named organisational-psychology studies, effect sizes or dated employer-survey figures on managing employees high in negative affectivity or social inhibition: which specific manager practices measurably improve their performance, engagement or retention. Look for one-to-one cadence and feedback-delivery research, psychological-safety work (Edmondson and successors) with reported effect sizes, task-fit and job-crafting studies, structured-onboarding outcome data for introverted or socially inhibited new hires, and research on how negative affectivity relates to error detection, quality-checking or conscientiousness at work. Prefer peer-reviewed sources and survey data from 2015 onward with real numbers attached.
